# Nebius verhoogt tarieven voor AI-rekenkracht met ruim 20 procent 

 Het verhuren van AI-rekenkracht in Europa wordt duurder. De in Nederland gevestigde AI-infrastructuuraanbieder Nebius verhoogt per 1 oktober 2026 de uurprijzen voor het huren van GPU's met 17 tot 21 procent. Dit blijkt uit de nieuwste Europese GPU-prijsindex van het onafhankelijke AI-onderzoeksbureau Lindstead. 

 

Door de prijsherziening stijgt het tarief voor een Nvidia H100 bij Nebius van circa 3,38 euro naar 3,95 euro per uur. De nieuwste generatie chips, de B300, gaat in prijs omhoog van ongeveer 6,88 euro naar 8,33 euro per uur. De prijsstijging past binnen een bredere ontwikkeling in de markt: de mediane huurprijs van een H200-GPU steeg in een jaar tijd met ongeveer 25 procent, waarbij elke nieuwe chipgeneratie duurder is per uur dan de voorgaande.

## Goedkoper dan bij Amerikaanse hyperscalers

Ondanks de prijsverhoging blijven Europese aanbieders aanzienlijk goedkoper dan de grote Amerikaanse hyperscalers. Uit de Lindstead-index blijkt dat het huren van een H100 bij Europese partijen zoals het Franse OVHcloud (circa 2,62 euro per uur), het Finse Verda (3,09 euro per uur) en Nebius ongeveer de helft kost van vergelijkbare capaciteit bij AWS en Microsoft Azure, en circa een derde van het tarief bij Google Cloud.

Naast de prijs speelt data-soevereiniteit een steeds grotere rol bij de keuzes van Europese organisaties. Lindstead wijst erop dat Amerikaanse cloudproviders onder de US CLOUD Act vallen, zelfs als hun datacenters fysiek op Europees grondgebied staan. Voor organisaties die werken met privacygevoelige gegevens zijn de eigendomsverhoudingen en het geldende rechtstelsel doorslaggevend. De lagere tarieven van Europese leveranciers maken de overstap naar regionale infrastructuur voor veel bedrijven financieel en strategisch aantrekkelijk.

results.title: Nebius Is Raising GPU Prices Twice in Three Months — That's the Clearest Sign of Real Scarcity | TOPONE Markets
highlights:
Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) closed at $231.88 on September 28, 2026, down about 23% from its June high near $300 despite second-quarter revenue growing 454% year over year. The company, a Dutch-registered "neocloud" that rents GPU capacity for AI workloads, announced its second on-demand GPU price increase in three months, effective October 1, with H100 rentals up about 17% and B200 up about 19%. That pricing power is the strongest real-world evidence that AI compute remains scarce rather than oversupplied — but Nebius is also spending $20–25 billion in capital expenditure this year, financed partly through convertible debt, and short interest sits near 19%, so the bull and bear cases both have real footing.

...

Nebius builds and operates its own data centers and GPU clusters, selling AI compute capacity, an AI cloud platform, and developer tools to AI companies globally. The company was formerly Yandex N.V. and rebranded in August 2024 after separating from its Russian operations. Its core platform is Nebius AI Cloud, supplemented by Token Factory for inference workloads, running primarily on NVIDIA hardware. This puts Nebius in the same category as CoreWeave and IREN — companies that don't build AI models themselves but sell the underlying compute infrastructure that model builders rent.

### Second Straight Price Hike Is the Headline Signal

On September 28, 2026, Nebius announced it will raise on-demand GPU rental prices again starting October 1 — H100 pricing up about 17%, H200 up about 20%, and B200 up about 19%. This is the second such increase within three months. In a market where AI infrastructure providers are sometimes accused of overbuilding capacity ahead of demand, a company that can raise prices twice in a single quarter and still expect customers to pay is making the strongest possible case that supply remains genuinely constrained relative to demand, at least in Nebius's segment of the market. Whether that pricing power survives if GPU supply improves industry-wide, or if cloud capital spending decelerates, is the central question for anyone evaluating the stock beyond this quarter.

results.title: GPU rental prices are going up, not down. | Peter Lee
highlights:
GPU rental prices are going up, not down.

Nebius raises rates October 1 — its second hike in three months:
• H100: +17%
• H200: +20%
• B200: +19%
• B300: +21%

Wall Street just split wide open on what it means. JPMorgan upgraded CoreWeave to Overweight ($125 target): pricing power, not debt, is the story — short-term compute now sells at a steep premium, some rivals at ~3x long-term rates.

Days earlier, Rothschild & Co Redburn initiated both CoreWeave and Nebius at Sell, calling neocloud earnings "cyclically inflated."
Both can't be right about durability. But both agree on the present: compute is a seller's market.

Behind the curtain, input costs keep climbing. Mainstream DDR4 closed at $46.11 on Sept 24 (TrendForce) — roughly 4x late-2025 levels — and HBM is effectively sold out for 2026. Memory, not GPUs, is the binding constraint on new capacity.

If you buy compute: review your rate card before Q4 renewals. The "GPU prices only fall" assumption is broken for now — and long-dated fixed-price contracts just flipped from hedge to liability.
Is this pricing power durable, or cyclical?

results.title: Nvidia B200 Price Hits $8.01/Hr as GPU Costs Diverge
highlights:
Renting a Nvidia B200 by the hour has no single market price, because Nvidia does not sell it by the GPU-hour and each cloud sets its own rate. Listings in November 2026 reportedly run from $4.11 per GPU-hour, the lowest listed on-demand rate, at Beam Cloud to $16.11 per GPU-hour. Google Cloud listed $16.11 on demand in us-west1 on November 6. Treat any single average, including one quoted from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, as a snapshot to check against provider pages. The B200 is listed as available for rental across multiple cloud providers as of November 6, 2026, and its status is active. It is no longer the only Blackwell option: HGX B300 systems based on Blackwell Ultra became generally available on Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped deployments on October 20, 2026, and Vera Rubin NVL72 is marked early access. Older B200 snapshots, H100 and H200 prices, and any one provider’s rate should not be read as the current market-wide B200 price. Check each provider’s current terms before you commit.

...

## Nvidia B200 Cloud Rental Prices Jump 79% in Three Months

The core data point comes from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, which tracks day-to-day cloud rental rates across a basket of providers. In late September 2026, that index put B200 rental pricing at $8.01 per GPU-hour, a 79% climb from where it sat three months earlier. That figure is a market average rather than a price Nvidia publishes or any single provider charges, and a separate October 2026 report from Uvik put B200 median rental pricing at $8.19/GPU-hour across 9 providers, a similar level measured a different way. The same analysis calculated that a B200 now costs 21% more per unit of compute than an H100, a full reversal from June 2026, when a B200 was actually 18% cheaper than an H100 on the same compute-adjusted basis.

...

H200 pricing sits in between, and its position tells its own story. The SemiAnalysis figures put H200 rental rates at roughly 1.76 times H100 pricing, a ratio that tracks closely with the two chips’ relative memory capacity rather than their raw compute throughput. That detail is the thread running through this entire pricing episode.

...

| GPU | Generation | HBM Memory | Cloud Rental (per GPU-hour) | Indicative Hardware Price | Approx. Cost per GB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | Hopper | 80 GB HBM3 | Baseline (index reference) | ~$31,000 | ~$387.50/GB |
| H200 | Hopper | 141 GB HBM3e | ~1.76x H100 rate | ~$39,999 | ~$283.68/GB |
| B200 | Blackwell | 180 GB HBM3e | $8.01/hr (+21% vs H100 compute-adjusted) | ~$50,000–$70,000 | Not listed |

...

None of this happens in a vacuum. High-bandwidth memory production is concentrated among a small number of suppliers, and 2026 has been a year of persistent HBM tightness across the entire AI hardware stack. Nvidia’s own next-generation Rubin Ultra platform has reportedly had to trim memory allocation per package because of the same shortage, and cloud providers including Nebius have already raised prices to reflect higher input costs on memory-heavy configurations. When the memory that feeds B200 and H200 packages is scarce and expensive to source, that cost gets passed straight through to the hourly rental rate. Nvidia itself has acknowledged the squeeze: on October 21, 2026, it announced plans with supply-chain partners to expand manufacturing capacity for AI infrastructure, citing extraordinary demand and constrained capacity.

...

### How B200 Rental Prices Differ by Provider and Billing Type

The $8.01 index figure is an average, so the price a team actually pays depends on the provider and on how the capacity is billed. In October 2026, Cloud-GPUs tracked B200 availability across 14 providers in 27 countries and listed B200 spot rates at $3.95 to $8.75/GPU-hour, while GPU Economy listed Google Cloud’s B200 spot rate at $1.45/hour. In November 2026, Modal listed B200 at $6.25/GPU-hour, Lambda listed an 8×B200 instance at $6.69/GPU-hour, and Runpod Secure Cloud listed B200 at $7.99/GPU-hour.

Older listings show how wide the spread already was. In February 2025, GPUTracker listed B200 spot pricing at $1.67/hour from Verda. In February 2025, GPUTracker listed B200 on-demand pricing at $3.40/hour from Vast.ai, and it listed Lambda’s B200 on-demand price at $3.99/hour. It also listed GB200 on-demand pricing at $6.50/hour from CoreWeave in February 2025.

Put together, these listings mean that spot, on-demand and whole-instance prices are different products, and a single headline rate hides that. An eight-GPU hyperscaler instance and a single-GPU marketplace listing are not interchangeable, so a budget built on the index average can be wrong in either direction. Before committing to a provider, compare like with like: the same billing model, the same GPU count per instance and the same date. Historical rates should be treated as history rather than as a quote, and a spot price should not be assumed to stay available for a long-running job.

...

Cloud providers themselves are caught in the middle. Neoclouds like CoreWeave, which made HGX B200 instances generally available in May 2025, and Lambda Labs, which built businesses around reselling Nvidia capacity, have to pass through higher acquisition costs or eat margin. Some have already chosen the former: Nebius, one of the higher-profile AI-cloud operators, raised its own pricing in 2026 citing rising memory costs, and it reportedly lifted its B200 on-demand rate from $7.15 to $8.50 per GPU-hour on October 1, 2026, a move and a price level that line up directly with the HBM scarcity driving the B200 and H200 numbers here.

results.title: GPU Cloud Economics: What a GPU-Hour Really Costs — Tom's Tech Solutions
highlights:
The 2025 consensus was that GPU-hour prices would keep sliding as Blackwell shipped and Hopper aged. That's not what happened. H100 contract prices went up in 2026, neoclouds raised tens of billions in debt, and the whole business turned into a question of financing. Here's how a GPU-hour actually pencils out.

TL;DR

- SemiAnalysis's H100 one-year contract index went from ~$1.70/hr (Oct 2025) to ~$2.35/hr (Mar 2026), about +40%, as capacity sold out (SemiAnalysis). The GetDeploying on-demand median was ~$3.39 in mid-September (Akash / GetDeploying).
- Scotiabank's model of a 100 MW GB200 NVL72 campus costs $40.3M per MW all-in and needs ~$2.91/GPU-hr for a 15% levered equity IRR. Cash opex is only ~$0.52/hr (Scotiabank via investingLive).
- At CoreWeave in 2Q26, depreciation ate 54% of revenue and interest another 25% (CoreWeave 2Q26). This is a capital-recovery business wearing a cloud costume.

...

## The market: prices went up

The Akash/GetDeploying tracker shows how spread out "the price of an H100" really is. In September it ranged from ~$2 to ~$12 per GPU-hour on demand: specialist clouds at $2–4, AWS P5 around $6.88, Azure's 8-GPU ND H100 v5 around $12.29 (Akash, Sep 12 2026). Spot and multi-year reserved run about half of on-demand.

The direction matters more than the spread, though. Hopper was supposed to fade. Instead, contract rates rose ~40% in five months because on-demand capacity sold out and anyone holding reservations kept them. When the previous-generation GPU gets more expensive, demand is outrunning deployable supply, and that's mostly a power and memory story (see HBM).

...

- Renting? Anything under ~$2.50/hr on a multi-year GB200 contract is probably below a new build's breakeven. Lock it in. Short-term on-demand above ~$4 is paying someone's equity IRR.
- Building? Your edge is cost of capital and time-to-power, not GPU pricing, because everyone pays roughly the same to NVIDIA.
- Investing? Watch contract pricing (SemiAnalysis index), useful-life policy, and interest coverage. The bear case is a tenant default hitting a single-purpose asset. Scotia compares it to fiber after 2001.

results.title: Data center GPU price: published rates, dates and sources
highlights:
In short

A data center GPU has no single price: an H100 rents at $5.191 per accelerator-hour on AWS Capacity Blocks, $3.99 per GPU-hour on Lambda, and $2.82 on the SemiAnalysis market index (April 2026). This guide separates list, street and contract price and shows which vendors publish none.

Line chart of H100 and B200 rental prices in US dollars per GPU-hour across cloud providers and market indices, each data point labelled with its source and retrieval date.

Key takeaways

- AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks lists an H100 at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions; a B200 is $12.355; AWS has announced new rates from 7 October 2026.
- Lambda rents an on-demand H100 SXM at $3.99 per GPU-hour; 1-Click Clusters run $6.16 at 16 GPUs down to $5.54 at 256.
- H100 1-year rental contracts rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, per SemiAnalysis.
- On-demand H100 capacity has been marked sold out on the SemiAnalysis index from February to April 2026.

## What data center GPUs cost right now

Three published figures answer the question as of 23 September 2026, each from a different price layer. AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML lists the NVIDIA H100 at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions and the B200 at $12.355 per accelerator-hour, with new reservation rates announced effective 7 October 2026 [1]. Lambda lists an on-demand H100 SXM instance at $3.99 per GPU-hour and a B200 SXM6 at $6.69 per GPU-hour [2]. The SemiAnalysis H100 spot-contract composite index, a weighted mean of observed rental prices across the market, stood at $2.82 per GPU-hour in April 2026 [3].

The spread between those numbers is not a contradiction. It reflects three distinct price layers, and a defensible figure names which layer it comes from. The accelerator itself moves the number too: the H100 is no longer the top of the stack, and the B200 and H200 carry different rates on every venue that rents them.

...

- List price: the on-demand rate a provider publishes on its own pricing page, such as Lambda's $3.99 per H100 GPU-hour [2].
- Street price: what market indices observe buyers actually paying. The SemiAnalysis H100 spot-contract composite index is built from hyperscale clouds, neoclouds, marketplaces and rental aggregators, weighted toward hyperscalers.
- Contract price: reserved or committed terms. AWS Capacity Blocks carry a reservation fee plus an operating system fee, and reservation prices are updated regularly with supply and demand.

Over the past year the contract layer moved sharply upward. SemiAnalysis reports H100 one-year rental contract pricing rising almost 40 percent, from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 per GPU-hour by March 2026, with on-demand rental capacity sold out across all GPU types in early 2026 [4]. Those are point figures from the launch article; the same firm's index history publishes the one-year term as a 25th-75th percentile range, which ran $1.45-2.00 in November 2025 and widened to $2.10-2.70 in April 2026, with the on-demand H100 row marked sold out from February through April 2026 [3]. The two starting figures are not in conflict: one is a survey-based point estimate, the other a percentile band from the scraped-market index.

...

Most accelerator vendors publish no list price at all, so prices surface mainly through cloud rental venues: even the strongest GPU in the world is priced by the venue that rents it, not by its maker.

...

| FuriosaAI | AI inference accelerators | – | 23 September 2026 |
| Graphcore | IPU accelerators | – | 23 September 2026 |
| Groq | LPU inference accelerators, inference service | – | 23 September 2026 |

...

| Intel | Gaudi accelerators | – | 23 September 2026 |
| NVIDIA | GPUs and AI accelerators | – | 23 September 2026 |

...

Where a number does exist, it belongs to a venue rather than a vendor. Google Cloud prices GPUs on its accelerator-optimized machine-family page, which lists 8-GPU H100 machine types such as the a3-megagpu-8g [5], while the general VM pricing page carries the discount structure: Spot discounts and committed-use discounts on most machine types (retrieved 23 September 2026).

...

Combine dated rental tiers with index ranges rather than single points. Lambda's 1-Click Clusters price an H100 at $6.16 per GPU-hour for 16 GPUs, $5.85 at 64 and $5.54 at 256, showing the scale discount a single spot figure hides [2]. The SemiAnalysis one-year H100 contract range of $2.10-2.70 per GPU-hour in April 2026 is a different layer from the same page's spot-contract composite index level of $2.82 [3].

...

On AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks an H100 rents at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions and a B200 at $12.355, with new rates announced effective 7 October 2026. Lambda lists an on-demand H100 SXM at $3.99 and a B200 SXM6 at $6.69 per GPU-hour. Over the past year, H100 1-year rental contracts rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026 per SemiAnalysis, and on-demand H100 capacity was marked sold out on the SemiAnalysis index from February to April 2026.

...

Because the quoted figures are often different products: a per-accelerator reservation, a per-GPU-hour on-demand VM and per-token serverless inference are never combined into one number. Region also moves the price: the same AWS H100 Capacity Block is $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions and $4.720 in London, Stockholm, Tokyo and others.
